claims.text: High defect densities and random local strain states primarily govern magnetocaloric response and hysteresis in as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type nanoscale alloys.
High defect densities and random local strain states pin magnetic domains.
Thermomechanical treatments can tune the relevant defect and strain states.
Argon–nitrogen annealing reduces crystallographic defect density.
Cyclic longitudinal tensile straining imposes controlled anisotropic strain.
Induced uniaxial strain modifies magnetic anisotropy.
Reduced defect density and controlled anisotropic strain lower energy barriers for magnetostructural transitions.
Lower magnetostructural-transition barriers promote more uniform and reversible magnetic-domain alignment.
More uniform and reversible domain alignment sharpens the magnetocaloric transition.
More uniform and reversible domain alignment reduces hysteresis.
Thin-film versus nanoribbon geometry modulates the effects through differences in shape anisotropy.
As-deposited films and nanoribbons have high defect densities.
As-deposited films and nanoribbons have random strain distributions.
High defect densities and random strain distributions produce broader hysteresis loops in the as-deposited baseline.
High defect densities and random strain distributions produce a less efficient and more smeared-out low-field magnetocaloric response.
Treated samples will show a statistically significant reduction in hysteresis width relative to as-deposited samples.
Treated samples will show a sharper and more reversible magnetocaloric transition relative to as-deposited samples.
Nanoribbons may respond more strongly to tensile straining than films because of enhanced shape anisotropy.
Magnetic-cooling cycle frequency remains constrained by heat-transfer rates.
